newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries may ease ahead of refunding - experts.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries may ease ahead of refunding - experts.

text.p: Prices of U.S. Treasury securities may face some turbulance ahead as a new outburst of fresh supply hits the market next week, analysts said.
The Treasury announced on Wednesday it will pour a higher-than-expected $39.75 billion into the fixed-income market at its quarterly refunding auctions next Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.
Wall Street pundits had expected the refunding effort to total $37.5 billion.
The refunding auction will be made up of $17.75 billion of three-year notes, $12.0 billion of 10-year notes and $10.0 bilion in 30-year bonds.
"The main surprise here is the size of 10-year being $12 billion instead of $10.0 billion," said Josh Stiles, bond market strategist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc.
On top of the size of the refunding effort, analysts said the Treasury market, which rallied substantially over the last week, is perceived to be a bit overbought at current levels.
The yield on the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond, for example, eased to a current 6.74 percent level from 6.94 percent on January 27.

"I think people might say 'Wait a minute. This thing is about 20 basis points lower than it was a week or so ago. Why am I going to be bidding at these auctions at these levels?" said Jerry Zukowski, economist at PaineWebber Inc.
"There is the potential the market is going to be hit a little bit ... From the supply perspective I think there is a chance for it to sell off," Zukowski added.
On the economic front, analysts said the wild card defining demand for the refunding auction will be the performance of the labor market in January.

Analysts said a weak payroll report might encourage some players to bid more aggressively at the refunding auctions. The January employment report will be released on Friday, February 7 at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.

Experts added, however, that a strong reading in the labor market report would increase the odds for a tightening of monetary policy by the Federal Reserve in March and, as a result, put some downward pressure on Treasuries.

"We don't want to see evidence that they're tightening further if we're going to sucessfully auction 30-year bonds," Stiles said. "I think the refunding is a tough sale at these levels without a friendly set of data on Friday."
Analysts said they expect activity on the when-issued market to pick up over the next few days, mainly after the release of the employment report on Friday.

"The bulk of activity in these issues ... will probably take place after the employment numbers and then early next week right before the auctions," Tony Crescenzi, economist at Miller, Tobak, Hirsch & Co, told Reuters Financial TV.
Analysts were also a bit surprised by the announcement the Treasury will re-open its existing 10-year inflation-indexed note when it next sells inflation-protected securities in April.
"We never thought they would boost the inflation-indexed 10-year after just having come to market last week," said William Sullivan, director of money market research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
"This flies in the face of the notion that the deficit is improving and they have less need to raise new cash," he added.
